title: Understanding jqXHR
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of understanding jqxhr in a jQuery application.
Apply the object returned by $.ajax() in a small example and describe its expected result.
Verify accessing response status with an explicit test or browser observation.
status_note: Draft generated from the attached syllabus and official references; requires lesson-by-lesson technical review, local execution, accessibility checks, and editorial approval.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will work through understanding jqxhr with a focused jQuery example. The subtopics below preserve the supplied curriculum coverage and connect the API idea to a small browser interface.
content.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it turns the object returned by $.ajax() into a repeatable implementation choice. jqXHR and Deferred APIs support callback-based orchestration. New code should understand native Promises and fetch(), using Deferreds when maintaining an existing jQuery integration.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local HTML page with jQuery 4.0.0 loaded before app.js for JavaScript snippets. HTML and package-manager snippets can be checked as configuration examples. Run the interaction in browser DevTools, inspect the DOM/Network panel, and compare actual behavior with the expected result. Do not submit learner code to the production API for arbitrary execution.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original markup and code, clear console/network filters, reload the local page, and repeat the same interaction. For a request example, return the mock endpoint to its original response before retrying.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with a known DOM structure, apply the pattern for understanding jqxhr, and test one normal case plus one edge case. Keep selectors scoped to the intended component and verify the real browser result.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Coordinate a pair of asynchronous outcomes around understanding jqxhr. Show success and rejection behavior, and compare with the native Promise or fetch equivalent.

task_acceptance_criteria: The implementation demonstrates understanding jqxhr using a current, documented approach.
The learner records the expected and actual behavior and checks at least one edge case.
The example preserves semantic HTML and does not render untrusted data as HTML.
The test setup and any runtime limitation are documented honestly.
hints: First identify which DOM nodes and runtime state are involved in understanding jqxhr.
Make one small change, inspect the resulting element or request, and compare it with the expected result.
If the result differs, check the selector, script order, browser console, event target, and relevant API documentation before adding more code.
content.expected_output: Uses native fetch and Promise chaining; fetch does not reject solely because the server returned an HTTP error status.
common_mistakes: Assuming a selector matched an element without checking the collection length.
Confusing jQuery collections with native DOM elements or live properties with markup attributes.
Using .html() with untrusted data or assuming client-side validation enforces server rules.
Treating a demo snippet as production-ready without testing failure and accessibility states.
summary: Understanding jqXHR is one part of the asynchronous programming and deferred objects workflow.
jqXHR and Deferred APIs support callback-based orchestration. New code should understand native Promises and fetch(), using Deferreds when maintaining an existing jQuery integration.
